summary: The evidence supports that structured exercise can be as effective as antidepressants for many people with mild depression. Meta-analyses and comparative studies repeatedly show clinically meaningful symptom reductions, especially when exercise is supervised and sustained. Results are not universal, so medication remains important for some patients.

sources.title: Effect of exercise for depression: umbrella review
sources.quote: Exercise showed moderate effects on depression symptoms across a wide range of populations and modalities.
sources.credibility_reason: High-quality umbrella review in a major medical journal with rigorous methodology.

sources.title: Physical activity interventions for depression
sources.quote: Structured physical activity improved depressive symptoms with effect sizes comparable to first-line treatments in mild cases.
sources.credibility_reason: Peer-reviewed meta-analytic synthesis with transparent inclusion criteria.

sources.title: NICE guideline: Depression in adults
sources.quote: Guidelines recommend considering exercise and behavioural activation as core options for less severe depression.
sources.credibility_reason: National clinical guideline from a leading evidence-review body.

sources.title: APA overview of depression treatment
sources.quote: Lifestyle interventions can help, but antidepressants remain effective and necessary for many individuals depending on severity and response.
sources.credibility_reason: Authoritative psychiatric organization presenting balanced treatment guidance.

sources.title: Comparative effectiveness of exercise and medication for depression
sources.quote: Exercise interventions yielded significant symptom reduction, though outcomes varied with adherence and study quality.
sources.credibility_reason: Major psychiatry journal with comparative treatment framing and quality controls.
